name: bluewater-tales-113-122
lines: The shopping cart was a flop. Nobody would touch it.
Oklahoma City. Nineteen thirty seven. Sylvan Goldman owns grocery stores.
His shoppers carry a hand basket. And when the basket gets heavy, they stop buying.
So he builds a frame on wheels that holds two baskets. The first shopping cart.
He lines them up by the door. And waits.
Nothing. The women say they have pushed enough baby buggies.
The men say they can carry a basket just fine.
So Goldman does not explain it. And he does not cut his prices.
He hires people. Men and women. To push carts around his store and act like shoppers.
And he puts a greeter at the door to hand you one.
Now you walk in, and everybody is using a cart. So you take one too.
Three years later, the waiting list for his carts was reported to be seven years long.
People did not need the cart explained. They needed to see someone like them using it.
He had to pay actors. You do not. You have real customers.
So show them. Where the next customer can see.
Two thousand five hundred years ago, a man wrote an insult on a vase. And we can still read it.
Athens. Around five hundred and ten BC. Painted pots are big business.
Two painters are the best in the city. Euthymides. And Euphronios.
They are rivals. And scholars think they were friends.
One day Euthymides paints three dancers on a tall jar. And he knows it is good.
So he signs it. Euthymides, son of Pollias, painted me.
Then he adds one more line.
As never Euphronios.
Meaning, my rival never made anything this good.
Then he fired the jar. With the brag on it. Forever.
Today it stands in a museum in Munich. And the brag is still there.
He did not write, quality pots at fair prices.
He said the one thing he did better than anyone. And he signed it.
Nobody remembers the painter who said, we do it all.
So what is the one thing you do better than the shop down the road? Say that.
The first vending machine is two thousand years old. And it sold holy water.
Egypt. The city of Alexandria. The first century.
At the temple door, people wash with holy water before they go in.
You drop a coin in the bowl. And you take a little.
But some people take a lot. For one small coin.
An engineer named Hero has an answer. And he writes it down.
A closed jar. With a slot on top.
The coin falls on a small pan. The pan tips a lever. The lever lifts a plug.
Water runs out. The coin slides off. The plug drops. The water stops.
One coin. One measure. Every time.
No guard. No argument. No sign that says, please be fair.
He did not ask people to behave. He built a way for it to work with nobody watching.
Two thousand years later, that is still the job.
What in your business only works when you are standing there?
Build the machine.
Captain Cook had a barrel of food his crew refused to eat. He believed it would keep them alive.
Seventeen sixty nine. His ship is months from home.
On long trips, a sickness called scurvy kills sailors.
So Cook has loaded barrels of sauerkraut. Sour cabbage.
The crew takes one look. No.
He is the captain. He could order them to eat it.
He does not.
He has it served at his own table. Every day. For the officers.
And the crew? They can take it or leave it.
So the men watch the officers eat it. Day after day.
Within a week, so many want it that he has to ration it.
He wrote in his journal that it was a method he never once knew to fail.
He never said, this is good for you. He let them see who was already eating it.
People do not want what they are told to want. They want what the people above them already have.
So who already uses you? Let the whole street see it.
A soap company once stamped its ad on real money. And people spent it.
London. The late eighteen hundreds. Thomas Barratt sells Pears soap.
He wants that name in every hand in Britain.
Posters? Everyone has posters. Newspapers? Everyone is in the newspapers.
So he thinks about the one thing nobody throws away. Money.
One problem. Stamping words on British coins is against the law.
But French coins are not British coins.
And a French ten centime piece is the same size as a penny. Shops take them as pennies.
So he brings in a quarter of a million of them.
He stamps two words on every one. Pears Soap.
And he lets them loose.
Every time someone paid for bread, or a tram, or a paper, they handed over his ad.
You can still find those coins in museum collections.
He did not ask, where do ads go? He asked, what does my customer already hold every day?
Find that thing. And put your name on it.
The word maverick comes from a man who skipped one small job.
Texas. Eighteen forty seven. Samuel Maverick is a lawyer. Not a rancher.
But he ends up with about four hundred cattle.
Every rancher burns a mark into his animals. A brand. It says, this one is mine.
Maverick never gets around to it.
His cattle wander off. With no mark on them.
And on the open range, an animal with no brand can be marked by whoever finds it.
So that is exactly what people do.
They see a calf with no mark and say, that's a maverick. Then they put their own brand on it.
His herd shrinks. His name spreads.
Today a maverick is someone who goes their own way.
But it started as a cow anyone could claim. Because nobody had put a name on it.
Your work is the same. The finished job with no sign out front. The van with nothing on the side.
If your name is not on it, somebody else gets the credit.
Brand your work. Or someone else will.
The man who invented the printing press lost it. Right before it paid off.
Germany. The city of Mainz. Around fourteen fifty.
Johannes Gutenberg has an idea that will change the world. Metal letters you can move and use again.
He also has no money.
So a rich man named Johann Fust lends him eight hundred guilders. Then eight hundred more.
Gutenberg spends years on one job. A Bible. The finest book anyone has ever printed.
He is almost done. About a hundred and eighty copies.
And in fourteen fifty five, Fust takes him to court. He wants it all back. With interest.
Gutenberg cannot pay.
By most accounts, the court sides with Fust. And Fust takes the type and the Bibles.
Then Fust opens his own print shop. With Gutenberg's best worker.
It becomes the first printing business to really make money.
Gutenberg had the greatest product in five hundred years. And he ran out of cash one step from the finish.
Being the best does not save you. Getting paid in time does.
So know your numbers. And never bet the whole shop on one job.
In eighteen ninety eight, a London store gave its customers brandy. For riding the stairs.
The store is Harrods. And it has just put in something England has never seen.
A moving staircase.
A leather belt that carries you up to the next floor.
Today you would not look twice. Back then, people were scared of it.
Would it throw you off? Would it pull you under?
Harrods could have hung a sign. Perfectly safe.
Instead, they put staff at the top.
And when a shaken customer stepped off, a shopman was waiting. With a glass of brandy.
And smelling salts. In case you felt faint.
So the scary new machine became the thing you had to try. And tell your friends about.
They did not argue with the fear. They did not laugh at it.
They stood at the exact moment it felt risky. And made that moment kind.
Every new customer feels that with you. A stranger in their home. A deposit paid.
So find your scary step. Stand at the top of it. And make it easy.
One ad took a beer from fifth place to first. And it said nothing new.
America. The early nineteen hundreds. Every beer ad says the same word. Pure.
Pure. Pure. Pure. Nobody believes any of them.
Schlitz is stuck in fifth. So they hire a writer named Claude Hopkins.
Hopkins asks for a tour of the brewery.
He sees bottles washed with live steam. Air that is filtered. Water from deep wells.
He is amazed. And he asks why they never tell anyone.
The answer? Every brewer does the same. It is nothing special.
But no brewer had ever told the customer.
So Hopkins writes the ads. Step by step. Exactly how the beer is made.
By his own account, Schlitz went from fifth to a tie for first.
The others did all the same things. He just said it first. So it became his.
You do things on every job that you think are boring. The checks. The prep. The cleanup.
Your customer has never heard any of it.
So stop saying quality. Say what you actually do.
Why do we call a sign of quality a hallmark? Because of a hall.
England. The year thirteen hundred. People buy silver. And they keep getting cheated.
A smith can mix in cheap metal. And you cannot tell by looking.
So the king makes a law.
No silver may be sold until it has been tested.
And when it passes, it gets a small stamp. A leopard's head.
Later, in London, every maker has to carry his work to one building to get it.
Goldsmiths' Hall.
The mark from the hall. The hallmark.
Now the buyer did not have to trust the seller. He just looked for the stamp.
Seven hundred years later, that leopard is still stamped on London silver.
Buyers have not changed. They still cannot judge your work by looking at it.
So they look for a mark from someone else. Reviews. A licence. Photos of the last job.
You saying you are good is just the seller talking.
Show them the stamp.
